title: What an AI Assistant Can Do for Your Work

production_notes: [VERSION] Product names Claude, ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Gemini, what each free tier includes, account requirements and whether each tool can search the web must be checked before recording. The voiceover only says that most have a free version and paid or company versions.
[REGION] Employer AI policies and the rules behind them differ by country and organisation; the voiceover only tells learners to follow their own employer's policy.
Tomasz and his Gdańsk warehouse are hypothetical; stock footage must not show a real company name or logo.
The voiceover makes no claim about how much time AI saves; learners measure their own time in the capstone.
Prompts appear on slides (scene 11); the presenter does not read them word for word as code.

Hook.voiceover: Think about your last working week. How much of it went on emails, rewording documents, reading long texts or making lists? An AI assistant can help with many of these tasks. It can also make mistakes that you must catch.

Explain.voiceover: Hi, and welcome to AI for Everyday Work: Documents, Email and Research. In this first lesson, we look at what an AI assistant can do for your work, and where it is weak.

slide.title: What an AI Assistant Can Do for Your Work
slide.body: AI for Everyday Work · Lesson 1 of 12

Explain.voiceover: An AI assistant is a chat tool that reads what you type and writes an answer in natural language. Well-known examples are Claude, ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Gemini. Most of them have a free version in a web browser or phone app, and paid or company versions with more features.

slide.title: What is an AI assistant?
slide.body: A chat tool: you type, it writes an answer in natural language. Examples: Claude · ChatGPT · Microsoft Copilot · Gemini. Free versions in the browser or app; paid and company versions add features.

Explain.voiceover: These tools learned from very large amounts of text. When you ask something, they predict which words are likely to come next. That is why they write so fluently. It is also why they can sound sure about something that is not true.

slide.title: It predicts the next words
slide.body: Your question → box 'predict likely next words' → fluent answer. Two labels under the answer: 'fluent' (green) and 'not always true' (amber).

Explain.voiceover: They are usually good at four things. Drafting, such as a first version of an email or a job advert. Rewording, to make text shorter, clearer or friendlier. Summarising a long text that you give them. And brainstorming ideas for an agenda or a presentation.

slide.title: Usually good at
slide.body: Drafting: emails, notices, job adverts · Rewording: shorter, clearer, friendlier · Summarising: long texts you provide · Brainstorming: agenda ideas, titles, questions

Explain.voiceover: They are usually weak at three things. Exact facts, such as numbers, dates, names, laws and prices. Recent events, which some tools may not know about. And your private context. The tool does not know your company, your customers or your deadlines unless you tell it.

slide.title: Usually weak at
slide.body: Exact facts: numbers, dates, names, laws, prices · Recent events · Your private context: company, customers, deadlines

Explain.voiceover: Here is a simple way to picture it. An AI assistant is like a fast, well-read new colleague on their first day. They can write a clear draft in seconds.
Explain.stock_query: new employee first day office welcome

Explain.voiceover: But they do not yet know your company or how your team works, and sometimes they guess instead of saying I don't know. You would welcome their help. But you would check their work before it goes out with your name on it.
Explain.stock_query: colleague reviewing printed draft at desk
Explain.on_screen_text: Welcome the help. Check the work.

Explain.voiceover: Two safety rules start today and run through the whole course. First, do not paste confidential or personal data into free AI tools. That means customer names, colleague details, passwords or unreleased figures. Second, follow your employer's AI policy, because rules differ between organisations and countries.

slide.title: Two safety rules from day one
slide.body: 1. No confidential or personal data in free tools: customer names, colleague details, passwords, unreleased figures. 2. Follow your employer's AI policy. Shield icon.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's see this at work. Tomasz is a logistics coordinator in Gdańsk, in Poland. On Monday, he tries a free AI assistant on three small tasks from his week.

First, an out-of-office message. He asks for a short, polite message that says he is away from Monday to Wednesday, and that urgent questions go to the shift supervisor. The answer is useful as it is. He changes one word and uses it.

slide.title: Task 1: Out-of-office message
slide.body: Prompt: Write a short, polite out-of-office message. I am away Monday to Wednesday. Urgent questions go to the shift supervisor. Result badge: Useful as it was (green tick).

Demonstrate.voiceover: Second, ideas for a team meeting. He asks for five ideas to make the weekly shift handover shorter. Three ideas are useful. Two do not fit his warehouse, because the tool does not know how his team works.

slide.title: Task 2: Meeting ideas
slide.body: Five idea cards: three with green ticks (useful), two with grey crosses labelled 'does not fit our warehouse'.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Third, a fact question. He asks which rules apply to driver rest times in his country. The answer sounds confident. But Tomasz cannot tell whether it is current or correct. So he checks the official source instead, and does not rely on the AI answer.

slide.title: Task 3: A fact question
slide.body: Question 'Driver rest time rules?' → confident AI answer with amber question mark → arrow to 'Check the official source' (document icon with green tick).

Demonstrate.voiceover: Tomasz writes a short note to himself. Good for drafts and ideas. Not reliable for rules and facts. Always check.
Demonstrate.on_screen_text: Drafts and ideas: yes. Facts: check.

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to treat an AI assistant like a search engine, or an expert that always knows the answer. It predicts likely text, so a wrong answer can look just as polished as a right one. Use it for drafts, rewording, summaries and ideas, and check every fact, number, name and date.

slide.title: Not a search engine
slide.body: Left: 'Expert that always knows' (crossed out). Right: 'Writer that predicts likely text' with a checklist: facts · numbers · names · dates.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, AI assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot and Gemini are good at drafting, rewording, summarising and brainstorming. Second, they are weak at exact facts, recent events and your private work context, and they can sound confident when they are wrong. Third, keep confidential data out, follow your employer's policy, and check the output before you use it.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Good at drafting, rewording, summarising, brainstorming. 2. Weak at exact facts, recent events, your private context. 3. No confidential data · follow your policy · check the output.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, try a free AI assistant on three small tasks from your real week, with no names or confidential details. Rate each answer, and circle any facts you would need to check. It takes about twenty minutes. The next lesson is Writing Clear Prompts: Task, Context, Format, Examples. See you there.
